title: Pagination patterns (offset vs cursor, total count tradeoffs)
hook: Clients ask for page 500 of a million-row table — offset pagination scans and discards 10,000 rows. Total count queries can double database load. Cursor pagination fixes deep pages but changes your API contract.

blocks.text: Pagination splits large result sets into pages. Offset pagination uses Skip((page-1)*pageSize).Take(pageSize) — simple but slow on deep pages because the database still scans skipped rows. Cursor (keyset) pagination uses WHERE id > @lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT @pageSize — constant time regardless of depth. Total count (SELECT COUNT(*)) powers 'Page 3 of 47' UIs but adds a full table scan or index scan on every request. Production APIs often return next-cursor links without total count, or cache approximate counts.

entries.plainDefinition: Skip N rows then take M — page number based.
Fetch rows after a stable sort key from the previous page.
COUNT(*) query for total pages — expensive on large filtered tables.
Unique, indexed column(s) for cursor — typically Id or (CreatedAt, Id).
entries.example: Composite cursor prevents ties when CreatedAt duplicates.

blocks.text: Pagination is on every list endpoint interview. Seniors must explain offset vs cursor tradeoffs, why COUNT(*) hurts at scale, and how to paginate filtered/sorted lists without duplicates across pages. Reddit r/dotnet frequently discusses 'should I return total count' — the answer depends on UX needs vs database cost. Missing indexes on sort columns turns pagination into full table scans.

blocks.title: Index the sort column
blocks.body: Cursor pagination on OrderBy(CreatedAt) requires an index on CreatedAt (ideally composite with Id). Without it, every page is a sequential scan.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Estimate table size and depth
items.body: Admin UI with page numbers on 50 rows — offset OK. Infinite scroll on millions — cursor required.

items.title: Define stable sort
items.body: Always OrderBy before Skip/Take or cursor filter. Tie-breaker column prevents gaps/duplicates.

items.title: Decide on total count
items.body: Need 'total pages'? Pay COUNT cost or use approximate/cached count. Mobile feeds often skip count entirely.

items.title: Project to DTO
items.body: Select only list fields — pagination + projection is the efficient default.

items.title: Return metadata
items.body: Offset: page, pageSize, hasNext. Cursor: nextCursor, hasMore — opaque encoded cursor token.

snippet.label: Offset pagination with optional total count
snippet.explanation: CountAsync runs separate SELECT COUNT — doubles DB work per request. Skip/Take degrades on deep pages. Fine for small admin tables; avoid on public feeds at scale.

snippet.label: Cursor (keyset) pagination
snippet.explanation: Composite cursor (CreatedAt, Id) handles ties. Take pageSize+1 to detect hasMore without COUNT. Each page is index seek — O(pageSize) regardless of depth.

snippet.label: Total count tradeoffs — cache and approximate
snippet.explanation: COUNT on filtered million-row table on every list request is a common bottleneck. Cache invalidates on writes or accept stale totals. Approximate counts OK for dashboards.

snippet.label: Diagnostics — pagination performance
snippet.explanation: Prove index usage with EXPLAIN in staging. Load test shallow vs deep offset pages — cliff proves need for cursor. Monitor COUNT query duration separately in APM.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Skip/Take without OrderBy — non-deterministic pages. Cursor on non-unique sort column without tie-breaker — duplicate/missing rows across pages. COUNT(*) on every infinite-scroll request. pageSize unbounded — client sends pageSize=100000. Offset pagination on user-facing feeds with millions of rows.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: APM compare p95 for page=1 vs page=100 on same endpoint — offset cliff is definitive. Database slow query log flags ORDER BY ... OFFSET large N. Index recommendations: composite index matching WHERE + ORDER BY columns (filter Status, sort CreatedAt, Id). For total count tradeoff: measure COUNT query as % of list endpoint time — if >30%, remove or cache. OpenTelemetry span per CountAsync vs data query shows double round trip.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Only knowing Skip/Take without cursor alternative. Ignoring total count cost — 'just add CountAsync'. No stable sort key in cursor design. Saying pagination is 'just a LINQ problem' without index strategy.

interviewTakeaways: Offset Skip/Take is simple but O(offset) on deep pages; cursor/keyset uses indexed WHERE on sort key — constant time per page.
Total count tradeoff: COUNT doubles query cost — skip for feeds, cache for admin, or approximate for dashboards.
Production tip: composite index on (filter, sort, id); load test deep offset; separate APM spans for count vs data.

60s: Small tables — offset OK. Millions of rows — cursor pagination with stable sort key and tie-breaker Id. Count is expensive — often omit or cache. Always OrderBy before paginate. Index the sort columns.
Follow-up: how do you paginate with dynamic filters and multiple sort columns?
commonPitfalls: CountAsync on every list request without discussing cost gets you rejected at senior level.
Cursor without tie-breaker on non-unique CreatedAt — rows appear twice or vanish between pages.

Strong answer: 'Admin UI under 10k rows: offset + cached count. Public feed: cursor, no count, nextCursor token. Composite index on filter + sort. I load test page 1 vs deep page and watch COUNT duration in APM.'
introducedIn: EF Core 1.0; filtered CountAsync in EF Core 5+

jsTsCorrelations.note: Prisma cursor API (cursor: { id }, skip: 1, take: 20) maps directly to EF keyset pattern. Same index and stable-sort requirements apply.
Relay cursor spec (edges, pageInfo) is the industry standard for cursor pagination — EF keyset maps to after/before cursors. Offset in GraphQL is similarly discouraged at depth.
